en: Bringing hardship upon China,
Your adversary Kakan-Chin—
If we wage holy war against Beijing,
Leveling it flatter than a palm,
Making springtime seem no more than autumn.
The army marching in a mass,
The earth hidden in haze,
Dust flying into the sky.
The march becoming a wondrous road,
The whole world stirring,
The army surging and spilling forth,
In the eyes of Kalcha Kongurbai,
Appearing like a monster—
Thus let us go to Beijing.
Against the seething unbelievers,
Against hero Khan Kongurbai,
Thus let us wage war!
When Muslims set out on holy war,
My only support, hear this:
Such is the nature of battle!
Raising the white sacred banner,
Shouting the cry of “Manas!”
With the white-mottled standard as our banner,
With plentiful shouts and uproar,
When we meet the Chinese,
The bronze cannon booming,
When the hosts meet in full,
When the general battle begins,
The battle-axes clanging,
Sharpened swords flashing,
Spears breaking apart,
Human blood spilling,
Ah, my foal,
A man's valor
Appearing like a lion.
When the facing enemy is scattered,
My only son of a hero,
Is that not a mighty marvel!
While my hero Manas lived,
With hero Bakai before us,
We brought calamity thus;
Crushing the enemy we faced,
We took them within a single day.
If death came, we died;
All those we faced,
When we advanced, we burned like fire.
While my gray wolf Manas lived,
I reclined in armor no bullet pierced,
And when they provoked me,
I crushed the Kyzylbash.
While bloodthirsty Manas lived,
I reclined wearing my shield,
And when they angered me,
I smashed and ruined the Chinese.
While your comrade lived,
Their gold, silver, and daughters—
Alas, what a woeful, dreadful day,
Why did I not die while plundering them!
Chinmachin and the Kakan,
Why did I not die while plundering them!
Making the Manchu crash,
Why did I not die while striking them!
When we seized the Kakan's khanate,
Why did I not die!
When we brought chaos upon Beijing,
Why did I not die!
Gripping a spear and breaking formations,
Why did I not die in battle!
In the mace-blows of the general melee,
Why did I not die in combat!
You have halted me at the frontier,
My young hero, son of Manas,
And made me mourn the old days!
Counting all that came before,
I sit here overturned with grief!
Against the seething Chinese Kakan,
When we charged and began war,
When we seized his khanate,
Alas, what a desolate day,
Why did I not die there!
When I poured my courage
Out against the Chinese,
When my humanity
Overflowed from my head,
Why did I not die there!
When, with courage, I hemmed in
The Kalmak,
When I struck
The Kaldai and Zuntung,
Why did I not die there!
When I smashed those who opposed me,
And cut them down,
When I inflicted humiliation
Upon the Kalmak like sheep,
Why did I not die then!
Filled out like a lion,
In your holy uncle Bakai
The old anguish stirred!
When my journey grew feeble,
My young son Semetey,
Do not make my days turn yellow.
While my gray wolf Manas lived,
He waged holy war in many lands,
And always heeded
The words of your holy uncle Bakai.
While my gray wolf Manas lived,
I raised the banner in many lands;
Defending the Kyrgyz people,
Taking the blue-mottled spear in hand,
I speared and shattered many lands.
While my accomplished gray wolf lived,
I girded the jekene at my waist,
And amid enemies covering the earth,
I rode alone through them and attacked.
Since my accomplished Manas died,
I am dead, not living;
Weeping long for my bloodthirsty hero,
My poor soul has seen hell while alive.
Reason has left me,
From weeping long for my magnanimous lord,
The light has left my eyes.
When my lion died,
My black beard turned white;
For your mountain-like uncle Bakai,
The end of days has nearly come.
I have spoken all these words—understand;
My needed only one, heed me!
Unbeliever and Muslim—
Noble orphan, think!
Such is the nature of battle.
Your uncle, dear hero Bakai—
An iron coat no bullet pierced,
Do you think he did not wear it?!
In the holy war where peoples clashed,
Do you think Bakai did not march
At the head of the people?!
The many people of forty Chinese tribes,
Do you think he did not know them?!
The sable cap upon one's head—
Who has not worn it at a jaunty tilt,
Who, while fortune was theirs,
Did not stride about roaring?
I have told many of its secrets;
Such is the nature of Beijing!
My heroic son, understand,
And heed me without making me wail!
Beijing is no easy place;
Those who go there to die
Are not a people it restores!
In that Beijing,
Of the great men of old,
None went and exacted judgment;
Whoever attacked the people
Of Kakan-Chin did not survive.
Solomon did not exact judgment there;
That is formidable Beijing!
Unfolding its nature from the root,
I have told it to you!
What he knew and perceived,
Hero Bakai told thus;
What he had seen and knew,
Hero Bakai told openly.
The young sultan, hero Semey,
Your hero who did not fear death,
Drew his arm back,
Your lion remaining unmoved,
His gray-wolf spirit roused, he cried out.
When he heard hero Bakai's words,
He summoned his two mothers...
Below Tört-Kül,
In the garden prince Manas planted,
Facing Great Talas,
At the edge of Great Ak-Chiy,
Within the walled stronghold,
In Chachykei's palace,
Hero Semey, son of the prince,
Your hero aided by spirits,
Külchoro, son of Almambet—
The ready expert in shooting;
Kanchoro, son of Chubak—
The strong master of the whip;
Argyn and Kyrgyz together,
Hearing Semetey would go to Beijing,
Poor heads were thrown into turmoil.
From the banks of Üch-Koshoy,
Sarykan, khan of the Argyn,
Heard the news and came;
A teeming multitude came.
Bölökbai, keeper of the treasury,
Leading his forty Kalchas,
(With his father, hero Manas,
He had been a friend unto doomsday),
He came raising a battle cry.
All the khans gathered,
The people came and assembled;
The khans wept in torrents,
The people grieved with a roar.
Sary Khan stood and said this:
“My only one left by the bloodthirsty hero!
Those who go to Beijing do not return;
No man has defeated it in conflict,
And no soul who went returned alive.
Toward harsh and perilous Beijing,
Pursuing your royal father's blood vengeance,
You have set out to grapple!
Return alive from Beijing;
Let them call you ‘the hero's son,’
And return safe from facing them!
To Beijing, whence those who go do not return,
My hero's only one,
You have set out in conflict!
With that Beijing, whence those who go do not return,
You have become enemies.
May your journey be through spear battle;
That you take no countless army—
At this I grieve.
Kongurbai in Beijing—
May victory over him be yours!
Toward Beijing that you face,
May your going be in the cool autumn;
My only son of a hero,
May the enemy you oppose be overcome!
May what you strike number six hosts;
May your splendid Bakai
Return as khan from Beijing.
My child, all else is false, but death is true.
Against the teeming infidels,
Charging with spear extended,
Let them call you ‘the hero's son’;
Now is the time to see
The calamity that comes upon your head!
Will a son not die for honor?
Will he not see
What God has inscribed for him!
Is it right to flee about,
Unable to avenge your royal father?
A man born for honor—
Can he remain unconquered without striving?!
Semetey, left by the noble one,
The mountain you lean on is iron.
Semetey, son of Manas—
Do not let them say he dwells in his village,
Unable to avenge his father.
If your doom comes, die and return;
If God's written decree
Comes upon your head, see it and return!
Of Chinmachin's Beijing,
The true lord is Kongurbai;
With the black-hearted Kalcha,
Grapple and spill his blood!
If almighty God the Creator
Created you by his will,
Go and break his ribs!
The enemy you must overcome is Kongurbai;
If your heroic father Manas supports you,
Bring him low and unleash conflict.
